speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture. Will the minister please inform the house what quantities of pork products are now held by the agricultural stabilization board? Will he also advise as to the intentions of the board respecting the sale of any of this product in Canada, and whether any of it will be sold during the present period of heavy hog marketings in such a way as to have an adverse influence on the hog market?

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: CANADIAN BREWERIES LIMITED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, stocks of pork products held by the agricultural stabilization board at this date are approximately 32 million pounds of pork cuts and 99 million pounds of canned pork. The board has just completed the sale, by tender, of about 500,000 pounds of ham stored before last September to be used for manufacture into a chopped, canned product. I am assured that the sale of this product for this purpose will have no adverse influence on the hog market.
The board does not propose to release any further pork cuts for sale in Canada in any form until such time as there is a more favourable balance between domestic pork requirements and hog marketings. In any case no cuts will be sold into the domestic market until after Easter. Board stocks of canned pork will be offered for sale in the domestic market starting April 18, under an arrangement similar to that followed in 1952 and 1953 when canned pork accumulated by the agricultural prices support board was made available for sale in Canada. The detailed terms with respect to this sale will be announced in due course by the stabilization board.
This sale of canned pork into the domestic market at that time is not expected to have any significant influence on the hog market.

Alderman Ostrander blamed three or four operators at the union stockyards who, he claims, are taking sick animals and turning
Inquiries of the Ministry them over to firms in Toronto and other centres. The alderman is also reported to have said that he was assured by an official connected with the federal health of animals division of the Department of Agriculture that culled cattle, many of them ill, were being sold, killed and cut up for human consumption.

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: TORONTO
subsubtopic: REPORTED SALE OF MEAT FROM DISEASED ANIMALS
speechtext:
The department is aware of the reports in the Toronto press concerning the allegations made by Alderman Ostrander respecting the sale of diseased meat in the city of Toronto.
The federal government has no jurisdiction over the sale of meat in Toronto in so far as requiring that all meats sold must be subject to government inspection. If meat is being sold in Toronto from diseased animals which have not been subject to federal meat inspection, the responsibility for dealing with this matter rests entirely with the local authorities.
The reports implied that diseased animals had been removed from the union stockyards in Toronto for slaughter in premises not under federal meat inspection. Inspectors of the health of animals division exercise authority over the disposal of diseased animals in public stockyards, including the Toronto yards. Inquiries instituted by the department following the statements attributed to Alderman Ostrander have failed to reveal instances where diseased animals were disposed of other than to inspected plants for slaughter under federal veterinary inspection and post mortem examination to determine their fitness for human consumption.
An observation that may be made in this connection is that a clear differentiation must be drawn between diseased animals and thin, aged animals, which are classified as culls but which are otherwise in normal health.

GOVERNMENT POLICY IN RESPECT TO CIVIL AVIATION
speechtext:
When the debate was adjourned last night I was referring to the competitive factor in Canadian air transport, as illustrated by Trans-Canada and Canadian Pacific Air Lines. I should like now to refer to some previous remarks I made because, as the house well knows, on a supply motion the opposition choose the field of battle, set up whatever straw men they wish, and then proceed to tear these dummy men to pieces. They can pick out those figures and statistics which support their case and ignore those which do not. Fortunately, having had an adjournment, I was able to do a little bit of checking on the expenditures of the transport department on airport construction. I should like to place on Hansard a few figures in that regard.
During the four years in which the present Minister of Finance has had the honour of bringing in the budget, the amount of money placed in the estimates for this particular item has been as follows: 1957-58, $35 million; 1958-59, $61,348,000'; 1959-60, $63 million; 1960-61, $52 million. The total for those four years is some $211 million.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT POLICY IN RESPECT TO CIVIL AVIATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, could I ask the hon. member a question, because I recall very well his figures yesterday. Surely he does not attribute the budget of 1957-58 to the new administration when he makes his calculations on a four year basis. Surely the Minister of Finance has only introduced three budgets.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT POLICY IN RESPECT TO CIVIL AVIATION
speechtext: The budget of 1957-58 was brought in by the previous administration, but it was this government that carried through that budget.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT POLICY IN RESPECT TO CIVIL AVIATION
speechtext: That is not what you said.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT POLICY IN RESPECT TO CIVIL AVIATION
speechtext:
As I have said, the total is $211 million. The hon. member for Laurier made quite a bit of the fact that in 1959 the amount for this item was $63 million while this year it is $52 million, a drop of $11 million. However, if one goes back to the four years prior to 1956-57 one finds that the figures were as follows: 1956-57, $15 million; 1955-56, $14 million; 1954-55, $10 million, and 1953-54, $9 million. The total for those four years is $49,350,000. If you go back even farther to 1952-53, the amount was almost $8 million for this item, and in 1951-52 it was $6.5 million. We find, therefore, that the expenditure for the preceding four years was a little less than one quarter of the amount this government has spent on airport construction in the last four years. The hon. member for Laurier says we are dragging our feet. I would suggest that the people who were dragging their feet were the previous administration.
I would suggest also that if one were to go back and ascertain the complete figures for airport construction from the time the Department of Transport was formed the total of the figures up to the time the former administration went out of office would not equal what this government has appropriated for this purpose. One cannot go back beyond 1950-51 because the expenditures for radio facilities and telecommunications were lumped in with this item, which is now carried as a separate item.
I believe the hon. member for Laurier quoted the Victoria Times to the effect that the airport terminal at Patricia Bay, Vancouver, was a glorified chicken coop. I would suggest that of all the terminals built by the previous administration, this is the only one that could be called a glorified chicken coop. The rest of them were chicken coops, and the only reason this one could be called glorified is because of the beautiful surroundings in which it is placed. However, I cannot say that the previous administration showed very much imagination or forethought in connection with the terminal buildings they did construct, in the light of the fact we are now having to replace them at practically every major airport across Canada.
The record of the previous administration with regard to the Vancouver airport is not one of which they should be proud. If my recollection is correct, in 1953 the hon. member for Laurier, who I believe was minister

of transport at that time, made the magnificent offer of $1 to the city of Vancouver to turn over their airport. Between 1953 and 1956, by easy stages, the amount involved worked its way up to $1 million. However, the city was not interested in turning over facilities which were much more valuable than that to the Department of Transport. The question was put to a plebiscite and the voters turned it down.
I should like to say a few words about the Vancouver airport, because I believe the operation of that airport under a local board has been a model of good operation in comparison with other airports across Canada. In the early days of air transport in Canada the city of Vancouver went out and acquired land for this airport, and in every respect were forward thinking in their decisions and in the actions they took. The situation now, however, is that the city would find it difficult financially to bring this airport up to the standard required for jet age transport. It is my hope that city and departmental officials can get together to ensure that the development of this airport will not be held back. I do, however, suggest that the previous administration was so preoccupied with centralization that no decisions could be made without reference to Ottawa. It might be well to look with favour upon a certain amount of decentralization in so far as the operation of these airports is concerned. Vancouver is a long way from Ottawa, and it takes quite a long time for decisions to be made.
I was told about a T.C.A. line maintenance building which was held up for nine months until a decision could be made concerning one of the three sites. Once that decision was made, all the details in regard to city negotiations were completed in some two or three weeks. I do believe that the airport at Vancouver must receive the backing of the Department of Transport. It must be built by the Department of Transport. I believe some consideration should be given to granting some degree of local autonomy in the day to day operations of the port.
The hon. member for Laurier had quite a lot to say in regard to giving away air routes.

The growth of air passenger traffic and air cargo will, in my opinion, be greatly expanded by a reduction in rates. Mr. Speaker, I am very glad of this opportunity to take part in this debate on civil aviation in Canada.
I think that Canadian civil aviation has done much for the expansion of our country and the development of our natural resources. We are also greatly indebted to private enterprise which, from the start, made great sacrifices to achieve practical results in that field.
We are also very much indebted to Canadian civil aviation because the federal Department of Transport made every effort in order to help private enterprise establish in Canada services which from the beginning greatly helped the development of our country.
Speaking of the Department of Transport, I should like-since we are talking about civil aviation-to praise all the efficient, capable and dedicated civil servants who through their advice helped private enterprise to make civil aviation what it is today.
I should like also, with all due deference to the members on the government side, to pay tribute to the Right Hon. C. D. Howe who contributed tremendously to the expansion of civil aviation in this country, besides devoting himself to the development of all sectors of Canadian economy.
I know that a few bigoted partisans do not like to hear the name of the Right Hon. C. D. Howe being mentioned. Just to show that I am not a bigot, I am prepared to admit that the Right Hon. C. D. Howe is a human being like anybody else, and that he possibly made some mistakes at the time he was sitting on the treasury benches; however, nobody can deny his immeasurable contribution to the development of our country in all fields of national economy.
Mr. Speaker, Canadian civil aviation plays a praiseworthy part in the country's development. It has made possible and considerably helped development in northern Canada. It has also helped our governments develop our natural resources. It has made possible and still makes possible faster communications between the remotest points in this country. It has rendered invaluable services to once inaccessible areas.

To come back to the Department of Transport's employees and before starting my remarks, I should like to give full support to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) when he said that we should give more assistance to department employees in this field. I think that the Department of Transport is now of such importance that the government should consider splitting up its various divisions. For all his devotion, his knowledge and his good faith, the minister now responsible for this department is not in a position, in my humble opinion, to carry out his duties adequately under present conditions.
To give only one example, civil aviation alone would require an associate minister. The field of civil aviation, Mr. Speaker, as I have just indicated, is so important that the people of Canada, and their representatives in the house, might well expect the government to have by now a well-defined policy, a wise, sound, intelligent and progressive policy, since the progress of civil aviation in Canada is closely bound up with that of our economy.
What do we find? An almost complete lack of any definite policy in our air program.
I will not say anything about our international agreements in the matter of air policy, since the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) has done so with a mastery that impressed the whole house.
Besides, this lack of policy on the part of the government in the field of civil aviation, began to take shape or to be felt at the time the government representatives were sitting on this side of the house.

I am confident that the material I have here will completely refute everything the hon. member for Laurier said yesterday, and this material was also in my hands at eight o'clock last night. I would have been equally glad to have gone on at that time. But the debate that was taking place at that time made it impossible. However, I am happy to do so today.
The introduction of these amendments to motions to go into supply seems to be following a new technique which has been worked out by the opposition at this session. They sniff around and find out which minister is going to be away, then they introduce an amendment dealing with his department so he cannot be in his place to deal with and refute the various points that are brought up.
If we went on that basis we would not be able to talk about anything.

Over the years that I have been here, that is some 10 years, it has been the accepted custom if an hon. member intends to attack another hon. member in this house he pays him the courtesy of notifying him ahead of time so that he can be here at the time.

speechtext: The question of privilege is that I had a perfect right to go on with this matter without advising the minister in any way whatever, and what is annoying the minister is that he was caught with his pants down in connection with it.

No, Mr. Speaker; the hon. member had a perfect right. There are a number of things that hon. members have a perfect right to do but, through custom, they just do not do them. I find that university students, like other people in this country, are very much interested in the dynamic, imaginative policies that this government is putting into effect, and are very anxious to have speakers from the government side speak to them at the universities. I accepted this invitation some six weeks ago. Perhaps the members of my hon. friend's party do not get many of these invitations. I was very glad to accept this. If the hon. member had had the courtesy even to phone my office as late as 12 o'clock yesterday or perhaps half-past eleven, I could have arranged for another speaker to go up and I would have been in my place at 2.30 p.m. The hon. member did not have to advise me of his intention to attack my department, but there are some things you do and other things you do not do. It just depends upon how you look at your relationships with your fellow members in the house, that is all.
I should like to point out at the very beginning that the purpose of civil aviation is to make it as easy as possible for members of the travelling public to get from one point to another. This requires the provision of air services, not the protection of air lines to the detriment of the travelling public, which was always the policy of the former government. The hon. member, in his amendment, particularly attacked the traffic rights which Canada has given to other countries, claiming we have given more than we have received. These particular traffic rights are called fifth freedom rights and are rights granted to countries which enter into bilateral air agreements, allowing them to pick up passengers in one country and carry them on to other countries.
Since we formed the government some two and a half or three years ago, we have negotiated several bilateral air agreements, and the fifth freedom rights which we have granted to other countries have simply balanced the fifth freedom rights which we have received in turn. To claim, as the hon. member did, that the agreements we have entered into cost the country some $5 million last year is

Civil Aviation
simply irresponsible nonsense. The hon. member's comments are a little like those of an individual who sets out to read a corporation balance sheet, and stops after having read the expenditures column, without bothering to look at the revenues statement. Like all good businessmen the present government has seen to it that expenditures and revenues balance in the agreements that we have negotiated.
In dealing with these fifth freedom rights the hon. member indicated to the house that the previous government did not grant those rights to other countries. He said that prior to 1957 Canada had a well defined policy in the negotiation of bilateral air agreements. It held generally to the position of exchanging third and fourth freedoms only with other countries, because to go beyond that would be against the national interest. That is the end of what he had to say in this regard. I might explain that third and fourth freedom rights are the right to fly between two countries who have signed a bilateral air agreement.
The former government claims that it did not grant fifth freedom rights because, to quote the hon. member's words again, "they were against the national interest". In fact it granted the following fifth freedom rights:
1.	To the United States at Edmonton en route to the Orient.
2.	To the United States at Gander en route to Europe.
3.	To the United Kingdom at Gander en route to the United States.
4.	To the United Kingdom in northern Canada en route to the Orient.
5.	To the United Kingdom at Montreal en route to the West Indies.
6.	To Mexico at Montreal en route to Europe via United States points.
7.	To Mexico at Vancouver from United States points and on to the north Pacific.
8.	To Australia in Fiji to Honolulu and San Francisco and on to Vancouver.
9.	To Peru at Vancouver, from Ecuador, Panama, Cuba, Mexico and to points beyond Vancouver.
10.	To Peru at Montreal from intermediate points to be agreed.
11.	To New Zealand at Vancouver from intermediate points to be agreed.
12.	To Japan at Vancouver to the United States, and on to Mexico and South America.
This is the record of the former government that granted, as the hon. member said, no fifth freedom rights because to grant them, in his own words, would not have been in the national interest. The hon. member either has a very short memory of what went on in the government of which he was a member, or he tried to mislead the house yesterday.

The hon. member dealt with what he claimed the present government had not done in entering into bilateral air agreement to make it possible for more Canadians to fly to more overseas points throughout the world. I should like to mention here just what the present government has done in this regard. The present administration has concluded new agreements with Switzerland, Austria, Germany and Italy and has renegotiated with the United States, the United Kingdom and France. I should like to specify what we have done in each case.
1.	Switzerland: under the Swiss agreement, a Canadian air line is providing service between Canada and Switzerland but no Swiss air line is as yet operating to Canada, surely no detriment to Canada.
2.	Austria:	under the agreement with
Austria a Canadian air line is operating to Vienna although no Austrian air line is as yet operating to Canada, once again no detriment to Canada.
3.	Germany: The agreement with Germany confirming existing arrangements for both a Canadian and a German air line to operate between their two respective territories and Canada obtained fifth freedom rights between Dusseldorf and Vienna and another point in Europe to be determined by Canada, in return for which we gave fifth freedom rights between Montreal and Chicago and either Boston or New York. In terms of traffic potential, this is a reasonable balance.
4.	Italy: Under the Italian agreement in addition to service between Canada and Italy, Canada obtained fifth freedom rights from Paris from Lisbon to Rome and from Rome onward to Bangkok. Italy obtained fifth freedom rights from Montreal to Mexico, Chicago and Los Angeles. Taken as a whole, in terms of population and mileages involved, these represent a reasonable balance. In fact, Canada is the only party exercising these fifth freedom rights between Lisbon and Rome, since the necessary permission of the third government has not been given in the case of the Italian rights. The establishment of Canadian service to Rome has not only provided direct access from Canada to one of the most visited countries in Europe, but has changed the whole character of the existing Canadian route to Lisbon and Madrid, and put it on a much sounder financial basis.
5.	United Kingdom: In renegotiating with the United Kingdom, the United Kingdom was granted access to Toronto in addition to Montreal which it had served previously, because Canada had access to the two largest traffic points in the United Kingdom, London and Prestwick, which had resulted in a traffic unbalance under the existing agreement. In

addition, however, Canada obtained substantial benefits-the right to originate direct nonstop flights in western Canada and certain fifth freedom rights from London to the continent of Europe. In fact, these are not small benefits, as suggested by the hon. member, but even though they may not be used immediately, are of substantial importance for the future. Moreover, out of the renegotiation with the United Kingdom has come also the major step forward in the form of a new pooling agreement between B.O.A.C. and T.C.A. on the north Atlantic, which will be of great benefit to both air lines and which is a direct consequence of the closer relations resulting from this renegotiation.
6.	United States: Renegotiation with the United States provided a direct transborder service to Calgary, which the residents of that city had for many years sought; and added a number of other new transborder routes for both countries which we believe will be of benefit to the public. The most important ones from Canada's point of view are direct access from Halifax to New York, and from Toronto to Buffalo. We are still anxious for even broader negotiations with the United States, but the whole pattern of our development of transborder routes has been one of slow but steady progress and periodic readjustment.
The renegotiation which this government has completed was in fact one for which the previous government had been pressing unsuccessfully for some years. Our whole objective is greater freedom in the transborder pattern combined with a willingness on our part to accept a greater degree of competition on transborder routes between United States and Canadian air lines, but the United States for its part must be willing to grant us a great measure of access to United States cities which we have not yet been able to serve. We will continue to press for this result.
7.	France: In our renegotiation with France we granted fifth freedom rights between Montreal and Chicago, and we obtained a full equivalent in return, namely fifth freedom rights between Paris and Rome. There can be no question but that the value of the one concession offsets the value of the other in terms of traffic potential, even though both may not be in use at present. Moreover, we have this same concession from Italy as well. On the matter of service between Montreal and Chicago, the fact that two foreign air lines are exercising this right will be of advantage in our next negotiations with the United States in dealing with the problem of direct service between these points for domestic air lines, and in fact supports our hand in this connection.

The hon. member also dealt with the opening up of the granting of B and C charter licences. First of all, I think it would be a good idea if I clarified in the minds of hon. members the different types of licences which the air transport board issues. The first is a class 1 scheduled operation, such as T.C.A., C.P.A., Maritime Central, P.W.A., TransAir and Quebecair operate.
Class 2 operation is also a scheduled type of operation in that it runs with some degree of regularity and operates in those areas where a regular service is required, but the routes do not have the first class navigational facilities provided for class 1 services.
Then there is the class 3 type of operation which is operated mostly in sparsely settled areas, giving the customer the opportunity to purchase his transportation for persons or goods on a unit toll basis. In other words, so much per person or per pound from one point to another.
The three types of operation which I have described have not been affected in any way by the change of policy of the present government.
The next class of service is the charter service, in which the customer charters an aircraft and pays for its exclusive use. There are three divisions in this charter service. The first is known as class A, operating large aircraft such as the DC-3 or DC-4 with a disposable load of 6,000 pounds or over. Operations under this classification have not been altered in any way by this government.
We now come to the class of service the licensing of which has been broadened by the present government's policy, namely class B operations which use medium type aircraft such as Beavers and Otters with a disposable load of between 1,100 pounds and 6,000 pounds. Then there is group C or light aircraft with a disposable load not exceeding 1,100 pounds. Whereas scheduled services are

of the nature of a public utility, the same case does not apply to charter services. The type of service provided by these charter operators is similar to that provided by the vast number of businesses which operate in Canada in providing services to their customers in the competitive field in which Canadian business operates.
For this reason the government some 18 months ago relaxed the licensing requirements as applied to C class operations, the fixed wing planes carrying up to 1,100 pounds and helicopters carrying up to 1,700 pounds. This new policy worked out very well indeed and resulted in no less than 128 new C class operators being licensed, 40 of which are at entirely new locations, thus bringing the benefits to a great many people who had hitherto not received this kind of service. In all the years previous to this only 75 operators of this class had been licensed by the previous government.
Because of the success of this policy with C class operators and the greatly expanded service provided to users, the government last fall decided similarly to relax the licensing of B class operators, and we believe that this policy will have equally good results. The government has made it very clear to the industry that only financially sound and technically competent operators who intend to carry on a year-round service will be considered under this new policy. In its notice sent to the air transport industry on January 26 last, the air transport board said the following:
Every applicant for a licence to operate charter or specialty commercial air services employing aircraft in groups B and C and helicopters is free to select any place in Canada as a base from which to operate. If the board is satisfied that the applicant has a bone fide intention to provide service at such base he will normally be granted a licence provided he can demonstrate financial stability and technical competence. Every licensee must own at least one aircraft in each group for which he is licensed. In addition, every licensee authorized to operate charter service must base aircraft in each licensed group at the designated base and must provide service therefrom on reasonable demand to all persons on the same basis.
The board will not grant a licence to applicants for short term charter services in the above groups, and must be satisfied that the applicant intends to provide year-round service on a permanent basis.
This government feels that it not only has an obligation to the air industry, but also to the public who will be serviced by the air industry. We believe that better service and lower prices are most readily achieved under the competitive system, and that this new freer licensing policy as applied to B and C operators will provide better and cheaper service to the public as well as a healthy stimulant to the industry itself. It is under this competitive system that our

economy in Canada has prospered and has provided the high standard of living we enjoy today.
The hon. member next dealt with our air terminal construction policy. He would know better if he took the trouble to compare the record of the past administration with that of the present one.
The contruction of a terminal building is no easy matter and involves many months of economic and technical study in forecasting requirements in consulting interested parties such as the air lines and inspection services and in reconciling conflicting views. Moreover, large terminal building projects involve not just the construction of a building but a great many other related factors, such as planning to suit specialized air line requirements, installation of very complex mechanical and electronic equipment, ancillary construction of major heating plants, substantial independent power installations, construction of hydrant refueling systems, ramp paving, and planning of a whole host of other projects all of which go hand in hand with a new major terminal building.
The complexity of this program, quite apart from the difficulty of meeting design and operating requirements in the rapidly changing aspects of aviation, means that a terminal project of this magnitude is bound to take longer to complete than the construction of a straightforward office building even of very large size.
The records of the program which I will outline indicate, I believe, that we have been making good progress in meeting the need for terminal buildings across Canada. New terminal buildings have been completed at St. John's, Newfoundland, at a cost of $625,000; Gander, Newfoundland, $3,500,000; Stephenville, Newfoundland, $425,000; Quebec, $660,000; and Windsor, $1 million. New terminal buildings under construction and nearing completion are at Halifax, $4,500,000; Montreal, $23 million, including aeroquays; Ottawa, $5 million, and Regina, $1,100,000. Tenders have been called, and work has started or is about to start at Toronto at a cost of $32 million, and Winnipeg, $10 million. Plans have been completed or nearly completed for tenders to be called at Williams Lake, $140,000; at Edmonton, a tender was called this month for $10,500,000. Plans are in preparation for tenders to be called at Victoria, $1,100,000; Prince Rupert, $400,000; Port Hardy, $420,000; Sault Ste. Marie, $658,000; North Bay, $450,000. Plans are in preparation for major alterations and additions at the lakehead, $650,000; Moncton, $500,000; Stephenville, $65,000, and Seven Islands, $55,000. In addition to the foregoing,
Civil Aviation
alterations and additions were made at both Toronto and Montreal airports and financial and technical assistance was rendered in the construction of the terminal buildings at Calgary and Vancouver during the past three years.
I ask hon. members to compare this program with the record of the former government. No one knows these facts better than the hon. member for Laurier, because, as the former minister of transport he was in close touch with these operations.
The minister quoted the figure for Stephenville. Could he say precisely what that was, and when it was spent?
Stephenville was opened in 1957, in case the hon. member does not know.
By the former prime minister.

It was opened when this government was in office.
The foregoing program amounts to a total capital expenditure of $96,740,000. This figure speaks for itself, and makes it clear that an extensive program of construction of air terminal buildings in Canada is being implemented. This is the airport program which the hon. member for Laurier said did not exist.
To accomplish this we have had to make major expansions in the construction, engineering and architectural staff of my department, in order to speed up the program which was lagging so badly under the static policy of the previous government. Increases of up to 50 per cent in technical staff were needed. Our estimates of $61 million for air services construction in 1958-59, $63 million in 1959-60, and $52 million in 1960-61 will certainly stand comparison with the $14 million voted by the previous government in 1955-56 and the $15 million in 1956-57, the year when they were on their way out.
The hon. member also asked why it was taking so long to repair the broken glass at Uplands. If he kept abreast of the press, he would realize that the damage to that building was far more serious than broken glass when a military plane broke the sound barrier last year, and may well cost up to $500,000 to repair. However, I am happy to inform the house that the Uplands building should be open by July 1.
In direct contradiction to what the hon. member for Laurier said yesterday, the Dor-val terminal in Montreal will be opened this year. The rate of progress for the construction of this terminal has speeded up greatly since the present government took office, and both our timetable and our cost estimates have remained unchanged for many months now.

particular to the hon. member for Victoria, B.C. (Mr. McPhillips) who is keenly interested in it. He is a very commendable member of parliament who takes a marked interest in matters affecting his area.
The hon. member for Laurier when speaking yesterday also referred to delays in bringing about improvements in the airport facilities at Winnipeg. I should like to put this matter in its correct perspective once and for all. I wish to draw attention to a press report out of Winnipeg under date of February 5 last which was published in the Montreal Gazette of February 6 and from which I quote with great pleasure:
For more than 20 years-
Please note, Mr. Speaker, 20 years. I continue:
-Winnipegers have complained about inadequate airport facilities. In response, federal authorities have supplied a generous series of plans and programs, the opium of the air traveller.
In 1941, Winnipeg was promised a modest $60,000 terminal. The new terminal was delayed because of wartime shortages but by 1946 Ottawa had conceived another plan.
Of course, the hon. member for Laurier was the minister of transport at that time. I continue:
After another five years, former transport minister Lionel Chevrier arrived here to say the new terminal would be going up "perhaps before another five years."
From then on, progress was comparatively rapid. Only a year later, another plan for $1 million terminal appeared. It would be under construction by 1957, said federal authorities. In 1956, just before the deadline, Ottawa produced another plan and raised the ante to $2 million. A year later, Winnipeg learned that a $5 million terminal was "in the design stage."
Year after year, the invisible new terminal grew in size and splendor. As they crowded into the existing terminal, air travellers could look north to a magnificent vacant lot and contemplate its glories.
Notwithstanding the promises of the Liberal administration and more specifically the promise of the hon. member for Laurier when he was minister of transport nine years ago that a new terminal building would be going up in another five years, the first contract for this terminal building was called by this government on January 15 last. That contract has now been awarded and work will get under way just as rapidly as weather permits.
I might also mention that in the case of three terminals put up by the previous administration within the last ten years, Moncton, the lakehead, and Seven Islands, we now have to plan extensions which might have been avoided if a more imaginative approach had been taken in the first instance to requirements.

There is no place for the stultifying influence of socialist policies in this or any other industry in Canada, any more than there is for the Liberal party's policy of supporting monopolies or vested interests.

Mr. Speaker, after the clear and concise report of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees), I do not find it necessary to deal with the matter, but I want to speak for a few minutes about the Dorval terminal, which is to be completed in 1960.

The precise date of completion for the whole project will depend on the way the work is carried out under the general contract and some additional contracts, for instance, for the installation of a feeding system for refuelling aircraft and paving the runways which will be done in spring. The first building contract of the project was given out a little more than four years ago. In the spring of 1957, the total amount of contracts was approximately $4 million. Contracts awarded since have reached $15 to $20 million. During 1959, a new runway has been paved, this being equal to paving 30 miles of road, 22 feet wide.
Though the lay-out of the jetties and the aeroquay was approved early in 1959, the
Civil Aviation
first estimate for the project seemed rather high, and several weeks were needed for the modification of plans so as to obtain the same basic lay-out at a reduced cost.
Plans for new passenger boarding facilities show twenty three aircraft stations on the landing area to which passengers will accede by following well lighted and ventilated underground corridors and passages. At each landing station, there will be rooms where air travellers will receive the necessary instructions and where they may wait for the time to board their aircraft. Air travellers will reach the gates of the landing stations by taking one or the other of two jetties starting from the terminal, or a tunnel leading to an aeroquay at the landing area.
One of the jetties with four landing stations will be used by planes for transborder flights. At the other end of the building are seven more landing stations for aircraft used for domestic flights. Parallel to the air terminal and 600 feet from it, is an aeroquay 1,200 feet long with twelve landing stations. It is connected with the terminal by two tunnels ending under the aircraft landing stations.
Aeroquay stations can be used by jet planes on international or domestic flights since an appropriate tunnel allows passengers to get to their own destination. All aircraft using the aeroquay, including those making international flights, could discharge or pick up passengers and refuel without changing stations, resulting in a saving of time and equipment for transportation companies.
The Minister of Transport referred to the charge that construction of the air terminal had been unduly delayed and he explained that the building of any air terminal of such proportions necessarily requires a lot of time.
This is due to the complexity of problems connected with the drawing of the plans, to the great number of interested parties to be consulted, and to the intricacies of construction and technical facilities. Two or three years are required to draw up complete blueprints and specifications and since construction itself will take at least four years, about seven years will elapse between the drawing up of plans and the completion of the project.
This delay in completion has been confirmed by the experience in other countries as well as in Canada. For instance, one of the largest cities of the United States has spent four years on planning but has not yet

It took six years to draw the plans of one of the largest overseas airports and six more years to build only the first part of that airport and at this time some changes to the building are being considered. Mr. Speaker, one could easily describe the twentieth century as the age of exaggeration or the day of the superlative. More often than not such exaggeration stems from habit.

I am one of those old-fashioned people who believe that competition is the life of trade.	When I support a policy which
restricts competition in any way there must be some very good reason for such a course. The air industry is one which meets this test. The air industry, unlike most other industries, has a special factor, and that is the factor of safety. It is true that ground vehicles have problems of safety, but they are of a different order from those which apply to aircraft. When it comes to the flying of airplanes and the carrying of cargoes and passengers, whether on scheduled or chartered flights, it is absolutely essential that there be no compromise whatsoever on absolute safety requirements.
We in Canada have a proud record in the field of safety. Trans-Canada Air Lines, I believe, is without peer in the field of taking no chances and of making sure that it gets

its customers safely from the point of their departure to their destination. So it has been with the air transport policy of this country, in years gone by at least, that in the field of chartered aircraft, too, no compromise was made in making sure that the industry would have a firm foundation which would not prevent it from being able to afford those things which are required to operate aircraft in accordance with the strictest safety rules.
This is just a matter of human nature. I do not think any person would deliberately reduce his efforts or slacken off in any way which would affect the safety of an aircraft. But on the other hand it is almost inevitable that if an industry is in trouble, if operators are continually losing money and if there is no other firm base on which they can build, there is a temptation to leave undone on occasion some things which should be done to ensure the safe operation of those aircraft.
That is the test which must apply. Here we have had a policy which only insisted that a person seeking a licence show public necessity, convenience or interest. In other words, all that was necessary for licensing was to demonstrate a requirement and then to show that the person making application had the capacity to finance and operate successfully the franchise for which he had applied.
This is a special category. It is something which is too important to trifle with. It is an area where, in my opinion, public safety supersedes the ordinary rule of unlimited and unfettered competition. Indeed, unfettered competition can, I think, mitigate against the service which would be expected and which would normally accrue from a more competitive situation.
It is for this reason that those of us on this side of the house have decided that the course of the present government in allowing unlimited licensing of class C and class B carriers is not in the public interest. We do not feel it contributes anything substantial to the service of the Canadian people. We do not believe it contributes anything in the realm of reliability; and we are concerned for fear it might detract in some way from a safe and sound operation of these aircraft carriers.
There is in addition the necessity, which always occurs in business, of making sufficient profit to allow for depreciation. The equipment which is required in the air transport industry is very expensive; unless it

can be depreciated it cannot be replaced. The funds are not available for replacement. Aircraft are not only expensive but usually the aircraft with which they are replaced are more up to date, more modern, more comfortable, but at the same time more expensive. Therefore the capital has to be accumulated from somewhere to take care of this replacement program, and only by having an industry which allows at least an adequate rate of return on investment can you build up the reservoir of capital necessary to replace out-worn equipment and to buy the latest aircraft available, and the best suited for the job.
This, of course, affects our aircraft industry too, because, as you know, it has suffered grievously in the last two years under the present government. It is all but wiped from the books, and any policy which will make it possible for domestic carriers to buy and from time to time re-equip their fleets with domestically produced aircraft is one which is of benefit to the Canadian aviation industry and which will provide continuous employment in that much-maligned industry.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I feel that the new policy which has been embarked upon by the Minister of Transport is a retrograde step; that it is not in the public interest; and that those recommendations which were put forward by the air transport industry are worthy of serious consideration and in fact deserve our support. Very simply, they were, first, that the federal government be urged to promulgate, without undue delay, a sound and well defined air transportation policy for Canada; second, that this policy should be of a long term nature and not be subject to fluctuation based on the exigencies of individual situations; and, finally, that with promulgation of such a policy full responsibility for its administration be placed in the hands of the air transport board. This final recommendation is also one of great importance. We feel that the administration should be lodged with and remain in the hands of the air transport board and not be taken over by the minister in a unilateral fashion.

Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock
I was speaking about the air terminal building at Uplands airport, Ottawa, and expressing disappointment over the fact that it had been damaged as the result of a flight of a FE-104 aircraft last summer. speechtext:
The hon. member for
Laurier said yesterday, as reported at page 1806 of Hansard, "I have no hesitation in saying that it was in 1953 that I announced the building of the airport at Dorval." In the first place, what were they doing before 1953? Back in the 40's? The government of that day was paying out the taxpayers' money for the development of a jet plane in Canada. They knew that the age of jet transport was coming. They knew that the airports in Canada at that time were inadequate to handle these developments, yet it was not until 1953 that any announcement was made.
I have to credit the hon. member for foresight in making that announcement in

February, 1953, but I am not sure whether his foresight was due to his realization of the coming of the jet age or due to his realization of the coming election in 1953. Nothing further was heard until November 4, 1954, when the next minister of transport announced that, so far as Montreal was concerned, there would be a $30 million expansion and modernization program for the Dorval airport. It is interesting to note that the Montreal Star of that date reports tenders for the work would be called that spring and the over-all project would take about two years to complete. That would bring it to about 1956.
In 1956, as every hon. member knows, very little work had taken place. In fact, when this government took over in 1957 the entire planning had to be reworked because there was in fact only a hit-and-miss plan for the airport at Dorval. There was, perhaps a reason for the announcement in November, 1954. Perhaps the announcement was made before the plans were well and truly laid, but it so happened that the minister of transport who made that announcement on November 4 was running in a by-election on November 8.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Again I think we have an example of foresight on the part of that hon. minister. I do not want to say anything more about the Dorval terminal. The present Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) has taken it in hand. The opening is scheduled for this year and finally, much too late I will admit, the airport will be opened. However, if there had been any foresight in the organization and planning of the previous government we might have had it opened many years ago.
Now on this question of air transport in Canada and the licensing of carriers, there is no country in the world in which it is more important that aggressive operators should be licensed than it is in this country. It can truly be said, I think, that more than any other country in the world we depend on the air carriers to open up our country, to open up the north and many of our areas of wealth which can only be reached by air. Yet the previous government for years followed a plan of restriction, a plan of monopoly, a plan of holding down individual initiative to keep Canadians from developing their country by opening up air routes and going into the parts of Canada that are difficult to reach by other means of transportation.
It was only when the present government came into power, as the minister said this afternoon, that a new policy was instituted.

The licensing of air carriers was opened up. Competition was introduced and the profit to the travelling public, the shipping public and those who want to open up our mineral resources and so on in the north has already been considerable. A country of this size requires a little vision. Hon. members opposite are apt to scoff at people who assert they have a vision for this country; but they do that because they themselves fail to have a conception of the possibilities of our country. That is why their policies were restricted. Their policies were policies of those who were afraid to look into the future. Their policies were: be safe and be sorry. Too little too late was their policy in airports, air carriers and in fact in much of their whole public thinking.
I therefore do not think that any member in this house need think twice before voting down these amendments and in effect voting for a policy that is long range in scope and has the future of Canada in it and voting against the old-line, old-time policies of do nothing now and only hope for the future.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to express my support for the amendment and the subamendment and to say that I will be quite brief and to the point, according to the clock, and will try to avoid exposing any ignorance. If no one spoke in this house unless as an expert on any question, this house would be filled with a profound silence on many occasions.
I must say this on behalf of this group. I want to protest the fact that I have not been allowed time to speak and to give the house my thoughts and wisdom, as I had intended to do, on this question. This group has had three speakers waiting all day to speak. Surely at least one of them should have been allowed 15 minutes. I protest the somewhat discourteous action of some of the other speakers who prevented at least one member of this group from expressing the point of view of this group on this extremely important matter today.

to the attention of the house a problem which is causing great concern to the people of my province and, in particular, to my own constituents. The problem to which I refer is the mass destruction of sea birds in our coastal waters by oil which is jettisoned from ships on the high seas and which drifts in and pollutes our coastal waters.
This is not a new problem. It became quite acute during the years of world war I and II when many ships were being torpedoed and a great deal of oil was being released on the high seas. In recent years the problem seems to have become much worse. At the present time it is much worse than at any time during the war years and has now reached proportions where some of the sea birds upon which many of our fishermen depend for food are threatened with extinction.
I realize that at first glance this appears to be an international problem originating outside our territorial waters, one that depends on international agreements and cooperation, and therefore one about which we seemingly may not be able to do very much. But taking a closer look I think we will find we are not quite as helpless as we may appear in this regard.
I should like to take a few minutes to suggest to the government and the house three avenues of approach by which I believe some progress could be made toward solving this problem. The first avenue of approach I would suggest is detection. There must be some reason why this problem has become so much worse in recent years. The ocean is a big place but it does not mean that the whole ocean has to be patrolled. It is well known that ships travel fairly well recognized sea lanes which constitute a narrow strip of ocean not more than 100 miles in width. Since this oil is brought to our shores by ocean currents it is only necessary to discover where these currents intercept the sea lanes to pinpoint the areas that would have to be patrolled.
We may have to carry out some investigation to learn a little more about the movements of these currents but if that knowledge is not already available to our hydrographic surveys branch I would suggest that we take steps to acquire it as quickly as possible. Once this is done I suggest we co-ordinate our patrol services, our planes, air services and ships at sea to try and detect ships that are unnecessarily jettisoning oil on the high seas. If we can do no more than find out and name the ships that are to blame I think we will in time build up a body of world opinion against this practice.
The second avenue of approach I would like to suggest is the scientific approach. It
Television Repair Practices should be possible to find some chemical with which this oil could be treated before being dumped overboard and, having been treated chemically, would sink to the bottom and not stay on the surface to drift around with the current. That might necessitate some international agreement so that the oil will not be dumped in depths of water that will interfere with our fishing grounds.
The third avenue of approach I would like to suggest is that our national research council might undertake, not only to try and discover some chemical that would be effective in making the oil sink to the bottom but also try to discover some mechanichal device which could be fitted to the ship's machinery and which could utilize this chemical so that the oil would be automatically treated as it is pumped out of the ship and thus not cause any further harm. If such a method could be found it would afford Canada some means of controlling this problem. We could then amend our Canada Shipping Act to require ships using our harbours and waterways to be fitted with this device.
If the government could follow these suggestions and develop some specific proposals to make in this regard then I think our chances of securing international agreement would be greatly enhanced.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal with another scourge which unfortunately we find in too many places across the country and particularly one which we face in this city. I am speaking about the unscrupulous television repair shops that by any device they can use will go into homes, obtain television sets, take them to their shops and then literally hold them for ransom. Apparently in spite of efforts made we have been unable to deal with this problem to date. I would suggest that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) look into the matter and see if the Criminal Code can be used to stop the practice.
The shop with which I intend to deal in particular is operated by a man who informs me that he services the television sets right here in the House of Commons.
In referring to the methods employed by these people I think the best example I can give is that just as communists use every facet of democracy in order to undermine democracy these callous, crafty beasts of prey use every facet of the law in order to flout the law of this country. They crawl like reptiles around the shadow of the law at all times; they never come out in the bright sunlight.

Television Repair Practices

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I wonder whether the hon. member is raising as a grievance a matter which is simply a question of law enforcement. It seems to me from what he has said so far that there are people whom he alleges are not observing the law. It seems to me that this is a matter of provincial responsibility and law enforcement. I raise the question, not to prevent the hon. member from raising a legitimate grievance but to have him justify his course before he continues.

Mr. Speaker, in the evidence I propose to present to the house I am sure it can be shown that under the present laws we are unable to deal with this situation. There are many people who have tried to deal with it but under the present laws apparently it is impossible to deal with these people.
1 should like to go on and illustrate just what I mean by this. Possibly the most reprehensible thing about this practice, is that these people prey upon the aged and the sick, upon the weak and the helpless. Television has been quite a boon to this country and particularly to people who are ill and who are aged and shut in but, unfortunately, television sets do not last forever and when some possibly minor thing goes wrong with them they have to be taken in and repaired. Quite often the class of people to whom I refer are working in the shops ready to pounce on the unsuspecting.
I should like to demonstrate a few of those facts. All we have to do is to take the telephone book of the city of Ottawa and we find this, and this is what I intend to deal with. At page 282 we find this man advertised as Addison Television, 791 Somerset street west. At page 283 this firm is advertised as CBS Television, at the same address. We also have Capital City TV Limited, same address. Then we have Capital City TV Limited again, and Cappy Television, same address. Then, on page 284 we have Crosley Television, same address; and Fleetwood Television, same address. Then, on page 285, we have Capital City TV again; and on page 286 we have Pye Television, same address. On page 287 we have Capital City TV Service only, and Capital City TV Limited; and then, so there will be no discrimination, again on page 288 we have for our French-Canadian friends the advertisement completely in the French language.
Last but far from least we have on the cover of the telephone book, which is conveniently passed out to most of the households in the country, the same form of advertising. This is an advertising device which is put out by the Dominion Merchandising Company,

Scarborough, Ontario. This cover goes to each community and carries an advertisement from one shop in each particular line. Television is advertised on the front cover of this book. The cover fits on the telephone book of the community you are in and it is distributed by this company to the householder. There are 12 traps set for the unwary. One further practice that I have seen in this particular shop is to use the advertising of the better business bureau after it has been kicked out of the better business bureau of Ottawa. Now what happens when these traps are sprung?
I had occasion to have some personal experience in this shop. Last week I discovered a situation where two government employees who were sharing a flat had some trouble with their television set. Unfortunately they got into the hands of this company to which 1 have referred. What they told me I could not believe; therefore, I took the opportunity to go with them to the shop when they went to have a look at their set. This is what happened. They called one of those numbers that I have listed, I do not know which one. A man came down and examined their set and changed one tube. He took off the back cover and said, "There must be some loose wire". He said he would take it back to the shop. He was instructed that it was a second-hand set and if the bill should come to a certain amount that he should return the set and not proceed with the repair of it. A week went by. They phoned two or three times. He did not itemize the bill and they were finally told that the bill was $47.80. They proceeded to get into an argument over it and he said, "If that is the way you feel the bill is $57.80, not $47.80". They asked for a detailed statement. He said, "You will get your statement when you pay your bill".
As I said, Mr. Speaker, I found this rather hard to believe so I took the opportunity to go with them when they went to see about it. I got a copy of the detailed statement, and when I started to read it the fellow made a lurch for it and tried to snatch it out of my hand; so I promptly put it in my pocket. He threatened to call the police; he threatened to attack me and the moment my back was turned his wife proceeded to do so in order to recover this price list.
I know it seems quite amusing to hon. members to picture some poor woman attacking a man of my size, but I should like to point out, that it would not be very amusing to an old age pensioner standing in my place. Such abuse and intimidation are the usual practice with these people. I have evidence here to prove that this is a general practice

and not one reserved for a particular occasion. I took this matter up with the better business bureau and I found that this practice has gone on for some time. The bureau was kind enough to give me a file which dealt with this one business alone. I should like to take this opportunity, to read just one or two of the complaints. This letter is dated March 1, 1960, and reads as follows:
Dear Sirs:
Saturday, February 27, 1960, I called Capital City Television Repair to pick up my T.V. which was out of order. The man came, looked at some tubes and took the set with him. Then several people told me that it was the worst place that I could have sent it to. It would cost me $50 or more to get it back. So I went down to pick it up again, when I got there the set had not been worked on it yet, I asked the lady if I could have it back by paying the service charge. They told me to wait till the man who had the record of it came back. I left for 30 minutes and when I came back they had the set torn apart. I complained to the manager of the store. He told me it cost me $15 to get it back, he wanted to throw me out of the store and even had a notion to hit me. I let him know he could not frighten me and I would stay till I had the set. Finally, they put the set back together and I paid $15 and left. I know now there are many complaints against this outfit and I hope my complaint will help to drive Capital City T V Repair out of business.
Yours truly,
The second letter reads as follows:
Cappy's T V were called in, after seeing their ad in the paper; they replaced a fuse and got the set working and charged a reasonable amount.
As the set was rather old, Mrs. H. asked them if they could tell her what it would cost to put the set in really good condition, as she wanted to know whether this would be worth while or whether they should get a new set. The repairman said they would give her an estimate and took the set into the shop.
When she did not get a call to give her the promised estimate, Mrs. H. called the shop. She was told the work was under way and the set would be delivered when ready. Mrs. H. protested that she had only wanted an estimate, but they replied that they could not do that sort of thing.
When the set was not delivered when promised, Mrs. H. again telephoned and they sent a man to get the chassis. He was to put the works in it and return it. Mrs. H. let him take it.
Mrs. H. then telephoned again to have the set delivered and was told that it was a cash deal and she should have $50.20 on hand.
Mrs. H. is rather young and inexperienced; it was her mother-in-law who came in and registered this complaint.
I might add, Mr. Speaker, that in the case to which I referred a moment ago and of which I have some rather fond memories, an attempt was made at that time to take the cabinet that went with the set. Fortunately, they would not give it up. I have just referred to two of the letters, but there are many more here. I am not going to take the time of the house to read them because 79951-0-118
Television Repair Practices I believe these two are indicative. Here we have a summary of eight different cases which range up to $120.
I have talked with other reputable dealers in town and they are all familiar with this particular case to which I refer. There is one thing I could say and that is in many respects these people are similar to rattlesnakes. Fortunately, there are two things missing. The first is that there is no rattle to warn people and the second is that, fortunately, they are not like the rattlesnake, immune to their own poison. The way to cure this is to have a fully informed public. There are two groups of our society that are involved here, the general public who are being victimized and the reputable dealers who are trying to do an honest job but who are being smeared along with the rest of the dealers.
I would suggest, that the general public should be advised that if they do not know a dealer they should check with the better business bureau. Second, if they are caught by one of these unscrupulous dealers they should immediately write to their better business bureau and complain or write to their member of parliament so that the complaint can be dealt with in some way. I would suggest also that the dealers themselves should try to clean their own house. They should try to set up some kind of ethical standards for dealers. I would suggest that the better business bureaus and chambers of commerce look into methods to put a stop to this practice either through municipal bylaws, provincial laws or, if necessary, urge the federal governmnet to amend the Criminal Code. I believe that the public should be protected, especially those who are least able to protect themselves. I would suggest that the Minister of Justice endeavour to see if there is something that could be done through the Criminal Code to deal with people of this kind.

I recall some years ago when this principle was established whereby the federal government assumed a large proportion of the cost of eliminating dangerous railroad crossings. At some later stage the federal government agreed to increase its contribution to the expense of eliminating dangerous railroad crossings. However, I should like to contend that even at the present time the burden that is left upon the municipal governments is in many cases beyond their ability to look after. We are planning the elimination of one of these intersections in my riding at the present time. While we appreciate that Ottawa is prepared to pay 80 per cent of the cost, the railroad company-in this case the Canadian Pacific Railway-is only prepared to pay 5 per cent of the cost. This leaves the municipal government with the responsibility of finding 15 per cent of the cost.
I feel that the government ought to undertake measures whereby the railroad companies are not left with an option to pay an indefinite amount. Rather I feel that the railroad companies should be obligated to assume a definite responsibility. If the government is unwilling to do that, this government will have to begin to assume an even greater share of the expense than the 80 per cent that now they are willing to share.
I think of one municipality alone, namely the municipality of Burnaby, which has a population in excess of 100,000. It has an urban area. Yet it has a main Great Northern railway line running through the heart of the municipality which incidentally is also used by the Canadian National Railways. There are six main roads across that railroad. There is Boundary road, Willingdon road, Douglas road, Sperling road, Cariboo road and North road and only at North road have we been able to eliminate, by means of an overhead pass, the very dangerous railroad crossing that exists.
There you have a municipality with five railroad crossings that need elimination. I understand that the average expense of eliminating one of these crossings runs in the

neighbourhood of three quarters of a million dollars. If you multiply three-quarters of a million dollars by five and then take 20 per cent of that figure, the committee will easily realize that the taxpayers of Burnaby would be obliged to raise over half a million dollars to eliminate only the worst of the crossings on only one of the several railroads that traverse that municipality. I contend that this is beyond the ability of real estate in the municipality to bear by way of added taxation.
I should therefore like to offer to the government the proposal that either it raise its own contribution from 80 per cent to at least 90 per cent or that it adopt legislation- amendments to the Railway Act or amendments to other legislation-whereby the railway companies would be obliged to assume 10 per cent or 15 per cent of the cost, thereby leaving municipal governments with responsibility for raising only 5 per cent or 10 per cent of the cost. Our municipalities are not asking to be completely relieved of responsibility in this matter. However, they contend that as conditions now exist they are unable to eliminate many of these railroad crossings that ought to be eliminated having due regard for the welfare and the safety of the people concerned.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a few words about this railway grade crossing situation. We had a problem in Brockville in the county of Leeds, and it has been a problem down through the years. I remember when I was first elected in 1953 that my maiden speech concerned itself with a problem which had existed for many years. I would like to repeat a portion of my speech which is to be found on page 5182 of Hansard for May 27, 1954. I said:
At times the traffic is halted for long intervals. On one occasion a car was rushing a patient to hospital when it was forced to halt until the train pulled away from the station, and the delay was for some time, but I am glad to say that the mother and child are doing nicely.
This matter regarding grade crossings was brought to the attention of the former government on several occasions. It was first raised in the middle thirties, in 1936 or 1937, but apparently the government of that time thought that Leeds county was entrenched so solidly with Liberalism that they did not consider they had to give the county town of Brockville anything to retain that support.

In 1953 when I came along as the representative of that county, I pursued every means possible to bring to the attention of the government and the board of transport commissioners the situation which existed at that time, but to no avail. Then in May 1957 I was never so humiliated in all my life as when the present Prime Minister visited Brockville in his private car. He pulled up into the station at Brockville and both he and his good wife, were forced to walk a block and a half over the rough railroad ties, in order to get to the railway station where a group of cars were waiting to transport them to the hotel for the evening speeches which were to follow. First of all we pulled around into William street and the gates were down. Then we pulled back to another street and the gates were down there. Then we went back again to William street and even then the gates were not raised. In all we had to wait for ten or fifteen minutes before we were able to proceed.
That situation had existed in Brockville for years and years; now it is even worse. There are three highways passing through, highway 401, No. 29 and No. 42, and it is necessary to come in through William street over the railway crossing which consists of 11 tracks. You may well imagine that when the gates are down the traffic is held up for 15, 20 and sometimes as much as 30 minutes, with all the inconvenience which results. Not only that, but we have schools there where children have to pass over the tracks, which is a very dangerous situation.
After the 1957 election I was again happy to bring this situation to the attention of our present Minister of Transport and to the board of transport commissioners, and I am glad to report to the house tonight that through the untiring efforts of our Minister of Transport and also the efforts of the mayor of Brockville we now have tenders let for an overhead pass, the work has begun, and it is anticipated it will be completed next July. I suppose that if we had had a Liberal government for the next 50 years nothing would have been done about it; but the present Minister of Transport is a sound, sane-thinking man and he realized the position which exists there at the present time. Not only that, but many of the hon. members who come from the west have come to Brockville and know the situation there. The Prime Minister has seen it for himself, much to my embarrassment, and I would like to state in this house tonight that the people of Brockville are delighted to know not only that they are receiving that overhead pass but are

receiving it from a good, considerate, Conservative Minister of Transport and Conservative government.
