Mr. Chairman, I would like to add some comments to the remarks made by the hon. members who have spoken on this resolution, which resolution is intended to extend the act for a further period of three years beyond January 1961 in order that the government of Canada can assist in great measure in bringing about throughout our country greater safety at railroad crossings.
This has developed into quite an item, and no doubt there are many reasons for it. In reviewing some of the reasons why this problem has increased so greatly, we could possibly find a rebuttal to the remarks of the Minister of Transport, the hon. member for Danforth and possibly the hon. member who has just resumed his seat. At some length they expressed how in recent years the expenditure to meet this problem in Canada has greatly increased.
With the growth and expansion which has taken place in Canada during the years of the Liberal administration, it is not surprising that the numbers of motor vehicles should have increased and that the dangerous aspect of the railroad crossing should have increased correspondingly. I have made inquiries of the provincial police in Ontario, and I have read certain reports of inquests, and it would seem that the danger has increased not only because of the increase in the number of vehicles but because the speed limit at which motor vehicles are entitled to travel has been increased, in some cases to 60 miles an hour. This makes it easier for a motorist to fail to observe the signal, of whatever nature, displayed at the crossing itself. In addition, we are told by specialists in this matter that people have, for some years, become accustomed to rely on the flashers at the crossings, and perhaps for this reason they do not take the amount of care which they should in approaching unprotected crossings. This is understandable, because we all tend to become used to a practice with which we are familiar.
I know that the railway companies have given a great deal of attention to finding ways and means by which the possibility of accidents at crossings can be diminished. One matter which arises from time to time in the consideration of those who have to sit on inquests following crossings accidents is the effectiveness of the air horns on diesel locomotives. It is said that there is a great difference in the warning capacity of these instruments as compared with the old steam whistle. Possibly some railway employees are reluctant
Railway Act
to give testimony as fully as they could in this connection. In any event, I believe that some of the funds at the minister's disposal, along with the money spent by the railroads, could be used to study methods by which the warning note of the air horn could be improved.
We have in my riding and, I would say, in northern Ontario generally, a doubly difficult problem with regard to railroad crossings. Our highways and, in consequence, our centres of population, are built in mountainous areas where both highways and railroads have to take advantage of the gulleys which cross the natural landscape. It follows that on a number of occasions there is only one course to be taken by both the railroad and the highway. When the track and the road intersect in the middle of a centre of population, such as Sudbury, a particularly difficult problem arises because neither can be removed without extensive tunnelling, or excavation. Whatever method is adopted, it is bound to be expensive, even if it were practical from an engineering point of view.
Important to my area, in the city of Sudbury, where the road and the railway both run east and west, this problem arises in particular at a crossing known as Riverside crossing. The railway company has been approached by the municipality, and the government has also been consulted. The file on this question is not yet complete, but I trust that a study will shortly be made in order to bring about a remedy to a dangerous situation and enable the workers of the entire area travelling to their work to enjoy the benefit of an underpass which is definitely desirable. In addition, we have a traverse which is known to be a difficult one, the Suez crossing, some three miles south of Capreol. Although this is not the busiest of crossings, there are two curves within 150 yards from the crossing itself, which make visibility difficult.
It has been said that the first consideration governing remedial action at crossings is that of the amount of traffic flowing at the particular point. I realize that this must have its effect when a decision is being made, but other considerations apply, and it is my belief that possibly greater emphasis should be placed upon the potential danger at the crossing than on the amount of traffic using it. The fact that a greater amount of traffic may be using a particular crossing does not necessarily mean that it should have priority; attention should also be given to the serious danger that might arise.
For example, there is a crossing in my riding known as the Coniston crossing in

Railway Act
the village of Coniston. This is not a crossing which carries a great deal of traffic compared with some others, but it is definitely one where visibility is hidden by buildings, and for that reason it becomes a dangerous crossing and one for which notification, or warning signals, should be provided. The Levack station crossing is another example. Within a short distance of the station itself a driver is confronted with a railway crossing, much of the traffic being hidden by the landscape, so that there is little visibility either from the highway or from the track.
Reports disclose that people have become accustomed to proper lights on some of the more difficult crossings and therefore I believe the department, along with the railway company, should seek to bring about more lucid notification of crossings at which it has been decided that flashing lights should not be installed.
In this country snow covers the ground for several months. Where a white cross indicates a railway crossing that is just a few inches above a snow bank there is not sufficient warning given to a motorist. Another method of cautioning motorists should be found which would not necessarily cost more than the installation of the present warning signs.
I am happy that the government is extending these grants. Recommendations should be made to the railroads about their continuing their investigations to render the airhorn whistle of the diesel engines more effective. They should also be urged to pay greater attention to the installation of proper warning signals at smaller crossings. Although it is important to have proper warning devices at all crossings the loss of life at a small crossing is no less serious a matter than at a major railway crossing.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to commend the government for introducing this measure to increase the grants for the grade crossing fund. I agree with the remarks made by previous speakers this evening in connection with the importance of this matter.
All hon. members realize the accelerated rate at which the Canadian population is growing and the consequent increase of the use of passenger cars.
Perhaps I may be permitted to refer to an illustration in my own constituency which benefitted from this fund. The city of Este-van is the only city in my constituency. Hon. members may be aware from press reports that as a result of the oil developments in Saskatchewan during the past several years Estevan has grown rapidly and is

now becoming the centre of the oil industry in that province. Last year, in October, there were approximately 4,000 wells in production in Saskatchewan, 3,000 of which are in the riding of Moose Mountain. This industry developed very rapidly and centred around Estevan as a consequence of which the city witnessed an unprecedented growth in population. In the space of about three and a half years Estevan's population increased from approximately 3,500 to approximately 9,000. As a result, the municipal officials of that city were called upon to provide immediately many vital services such as new schools, additions to public buildings, extensions of sidewalks and water and sewage facilities to such an extent that municipal funds were quickly exhausted and other essential services including the provision for public safety became a matter of grave concern.
The terrain to the south of Estevan includes a large valley. This necessitated the city having to grow in the opposite direction. Estevan grew to the north with resultant construction on the opposite side of the Canadian Pacific railway track which passes through that city. There was a consequent danger to the safety of the public.
Fortunately the government had substantially increased the grade crossing fund. Estevan was successful in its application to the government for a grant as a result of which construction will be undertaken of a modern underpass beneath the C.P.R. track. This will remove the danger which had existed in forms of traffic hazards in this city and alleviate the burden which would otherwise fall on the municipal officials.
There is another hazard at the eastern end of the city where the Soo line branches down toward the United States border. With the increased traffic resulting from the rapid growth of the city it will be necessary to ins-tal warning signals there as well.
In passing I might mention a thought which occurs to me as representing a hazard in Canadian transportation. I have noticed on several occasions at level crossings, especially in foggy weather, that trains made up of aluminum and stainless steel cars are almost invisible because they blend into the fog. I believe the government in co-operation with the railways should take cognizance of this potential hazard which has come about in the last several years since the introduction of stainless steel and aluminum passenger cars on Canadian trains. I believe there has been a greater incidence of accidents, especially in foggy weather, since these cars were first introduced. I recall that a serious accident occurred in Alberta last autumn in which this factor may have played a part.

I heartily commend the government on the introduction of this measure to increase the grade crossing fund. I believe the fund makes a vital contribution to the speedy elimination of many of the hazards that now confront Canadian motorists and pedestrians.

Mr. Chairman, I intend to be brief. I do not intend to make a Cook's tour of my constituency. I rise to bring to the attention of the committee a matter brought to my attention by a number of people in my constituency and one which was dealt with to some extent by the hon. member for Nickel Belt.
I am sure the principle and purpose of this measure receives the unanimous support of all hon. members of this committee and I suppose the only criticism would be that it is unfortunate we cannot spend more on the construction of railway crossings than we do at the present time. While there has been a great improvement since the increased funds were voted as a result of this legislation some years ago there is a great deal more required to be done to reduce accidents with their consequent loss of life and damage to property. Any hon. member who has read the papers will realize that even since coming to Ottawa a number of tragic accidents as a result of vehicles colliding with trains and vice versa have taken place within a few hundred miles of this city.
While we know it is usually considered that the greatest hazard exists in the populous centres I suggest that in some cases it does not because the people in populous centres are prepared for the crossings they encounter to an extent that is not found in the smaller communities and in the country. I appreciate that the ideal solution is the building of underpasses or overpasses but they are extremely costly in many cases. I believe consideration should be given to the increased installation of signals, bells and flashing lights at crossings.
Even in the constituency I have the honour to represent which is covered with mountain roads that are being rebuilt according to modern standards, owing to an influx of tourists in the summer there are great hazards at a number of railroad crossings. In my constituency we have what you might call country roads which cross a railroad three or four times in a distance of a few miles. My point is this. Local people know where those crossings are. Because of the paving of the roads and standardization tourists coming into the districts at high speeds can come on to those crossings without much notice.
The hon. member mentioned one serious accident which occurred this winter. It is not sufficient just to have white posts and a
Railway Act
cross stuck some distance from a railroad crossing. In constituencies such as I have the honour to represent we have five or six feet of snow and it is very difficult for a person driving a car or other vehicle, and particularly strangers to the district, to see that sign and be prepared for a railroad crossing. The same thing exists during the summer months.
This difficulty has been brought to my attention by a number of people, chambers of commerce and persons interested in tourist resorts, in the tourist business and so on. It has been suggested that without a great deal of expense-we all know the enormous expenses involved in those underpasses and overpasses-a great deal more could be done to protect the travelling public by the erection of, shall I say, some sort of dramatic sign. In that respect, I would suggest that the minister could follow the example of our minister of highways in British Columbia. There we have those large signs on the highway where construction is going on reading, "Sorry for the inconvenience because of this construction. Your minister of highways, Phil Gaglardi". I know this is a cheap form of advertising, but the signs, because of their colour and size, are easily noticed. Everybody notices these signs before he comes to the construction job and, to that extent, they serve a very useful purpose while at the same time advertising our minister of highways.
